guidance.heading: Choose on working load limit, not on size
guidance.body: Every part here is rated by its working load limit: the heaviest load it may carry in service. Start from the load and how it is rigged — the number of legs, the sling angle, how the weight is shared — and choose the component whose WLL covers the worst-loaded leg. Two parts of the same nominal size can carry very different loads: a Grade 80 hook and a carbon hook of the same frame, or a shackle loaded straight and one side-loaded. Proof and breaking loads are test figures; never select on them.

standards.heading: Design factors and patterns
standards.body: A lifting component is rated with a design factor between its WLL and its minimum breaking load. Alloy chain and its fittings are typically rated at 4:1, wire rope slings at 5:1, and forged shackles at 5:1 or 6:1 depending on the standard they are made to. Each size table shows the ratings the manufacturer publishes, in the unit they are rated in, and each product page names the pattern or standard its range follows — DIN 580, EN 13411-3 or the US G-209 and G-2130 patterns, for example.

service.heading: What ships with it
service.body: Every consignment ships with the manufacturer's test certificate. If your site needs more — third-party certification or witnessed proof testing — put it on the RFQ and we will confirm what we can arrange before we quote.

items.q: What is the difference between WLL, SWL and breaking load?
items.a: WLL — working load limit — is the most the manufacturer rates a part to carry in service. SWL, safe working load, is the older term and is sometimes set lower for a particular installation. The minimum breaking load is what the part withstood in test, several times its WLL, and it is never a working figure.

items.q: Can Grade 30, 43 or 70 chain be used for lifting?
items.a: No. Proof coil (Grade 30), high test (Grade 43) and transport (Grade 70) chain are made for tie-down, towing and general duty. Overhead lifting with chain calls for alloy chain — Grade 80 or Grade 100 — with fittings of the same grade.

items.q: Do the parts come with test certificates?
items.a: Yes. Each consignment ships with the manufacturer's test certificate. If your site needs more — third-party certification or witnessed proof testing — say so on the RFQ and we will confirm what we can arrange.

items.q: How do I read an Indus lifting part number?
items.a: IH-LR, then the family code, then the size. Inch sizes are written in hundredths of an inch (075 is 3/4″, 025X200 is 1/4″ × 2″), metric sizes in millimetres (10MM, M16), and capacities in tonnes (0T5 is 0.5 t). A trailing -C or -A marks the carbon-steel and alloy-steel versions of the same hook or link.

guidance.heading: Match the hardware to the load path
guidance.body: Rate every piece in the load path for the load it actually sees. A shackle or eye bolt pulled off its axis carries less than its vertical rating; a hook must seat the sling in its bowl, not on its tip; and a master link has to take every leg of the sling at once. Where a range comes in carbon and alloy steel of the same frame, the alloy version carries more — the size table lists the two as separate rows with their own ratings.

items.q: Which shackle do I need — anchor (bow) or chain (dee)?
items.a: A chain (dee) shackle is for a straight, in-line pull. An anchor (bow) shackle has a rounder body that accepts more than one sling or a pull at an angle to the pin. For a permanent or long-term installation choose a bolt-type shackle, whose nut and cotter pin cannot unscrew in service; a screw-pin shackle suits rigging that is made and broken often.

items.q: What is the difference between WLL, SWL and breaking load?
items.a: WLL — working load limit — is the most the manufacturer rates a part to carry in service. SWL, safe working load, is the older term and is sometimes set lower for a particular installation. The minimum breaking load is what the part withstood in test, several times its WLL, and it is never a working figure.

guidance.heading: A rope is only as strong as its termination
guidance.body: Wire rope is chosen on construction, core and tensile grade: more wires per strand bend more easily over a sheave, a steel core (IWRC) resists crushing and adds strength, and a higher grade carries more for the same diameter. Then the termination decides what the assembly can carry — a thimble protects the eye from kinking, clips must be the right number, the right way round and torqued, and a ferrule has to be pressed with the die made for it.

standards.heading: Standards for terminations
standards.body: Ferrule-secured eyes are covered by EN 13411-3 (the successor to DIN 3093) and lifting-grade wire rope clips by EN 13411-5 (which replaced DIN 1142). DIN 741 malleable clips are not intended for lifting terminations. Thimbles follow DIN 6899 and BS 464, or the US standard and extra-heavy patterns.

items.q: How many wire rope clips does an eye need?
items.a: It depends on the rope diameter and the clip type, and the clip maker's table is the authority. The U-bolt goes on the dead (short) end and the saddle on the live end — "never saddle a dead horse" — and the nuts are re-torqued after the first load.

items.q: What is the difference between a fibre core and a steel core?
items.a: A fibre core (FC) makes the rope more flexible; an independent wire rope core (IWRC) resists crushing on a drum and carries a higher breaking load for the same diameter. The size tables give both where the manufacturer publishes them.

guidance.heading: Lifting chain and everything else
guidance.body: Only alloy chain — Grade 80 or Grade 100 — is for overhead lifting, and it must be used with fittings of the same grade and size. Grade 30 proof coil, Grade 43 high test and Grade 70 transport chain are for tie-down, towing and general duty; DIN 763, 764 and 766 link chain is for fencing, guarding and light mechanical duty. The chain tables give working, proof and breaking loads as the manufacturer rates them.

items.q: Can I mix Grade 80 chain with Grade 100 fittings?
items.a: A chain sling is rated by its weakest component, so a mixed assembly takes the lower grade's rating. Match the fittings to the chain grade and size.

guidance.heading: Angle changes everything
guidance.body: A sling's rating is for a straight vertical pull. As the angle between two legs opens, each leg carries more of the load, so a two-leg sling at 90° between its legs is rated well below twice a single leg — the endless-sling table shows the drop directly. Choose the sling on its rated load for the angle you will actually use.

standards.heading: Wire rope slings
standards.body: Wire rope slings are commonly made to EN 13414-1, which rates them at a 5:1 design factor. The soft-eye sling tables give the WLL at both 5:1 and 6:1 so you can work to the factor your site specifies.

items.q: Are cable socks for lifting?
items.a: No. A cable sock is a pulling grip — it draws cable or hose through a duct or over rollers. Its breaking load is a pulling figure, and it is not rated for suspending a load.

guidance.heading: Capacity, lift and headroom
guidance.body: Choose a hoist on its rated capacity, the lift you need and the headroom you have: the hook-to-hook distance on the table is the height the hoist itself takes up. A trolley must match both the hoist's capacity and the flange width of your beam, and a plate clamp must match the plate thickness it grips — both ranges are in the size tables.

items.q: What is the difference between a push trolley and a geared trolley?
items.a: A push trolley is moved by pushing on the load; a geared trolley is driven by a hand chain, which gives finer positioning and is easier with heavier loads.

items.q: Can a snatch block be used for lifting?
items.a: Yes, within its rated load — but the load on the block is not the load on the rope. With the rope turned through 180° the block carries about twice the line pull, so rate the block, its hook or shackle and its anchor point for that.

guidance.heading: Bow or dee, screw pin or bolt
guidance.body: A chain (dee) shackle takes an in-line pull; an anchor (bow) shackle accepts several slings or a pull at an angle. Screw-pin shackles are for rigging made and broken often; bolt-type shackles, with a nut and cotter pin, are for long-term or permanent installations where a pin could otherwise work loose. Side-loading a shackle reduces what it may carry, so allow for it when the pull is not in line with the body.

items.q: What do G-209, G-2130 and G-213 mean?
items.a: They are widely used US pattern numbers: G-209 is a screw-pin anchor shackle, G-2130 a bolt-type anchor shackle, and G-213 a round-pin anchor shackle. Shackles sold to a pattern share its dimensions, so they interchange in an existing rigging plan.

items.a: No. A cable sock is a pulling grip for drawing cable or hose through ducts and over rollers; its breaking load is a pulling figure, not a lifting rating.

items.q: What does "standard lift" mean?

items.q: Can a snatch block be used for lifting?
items.a: Yes, within its rated load — but the load on the block is not the load on the rope. With the rope turned through 180° the block carries about twice the line pull, so rate the block, its hook or shackle and its anchor point for that.

categories.shortDescription: Ratchet, lever and claw load binders for tensioning chain tie-downs.
categories.seoTitle: Ratchet & Lever Load Binders
categories.seoDescription: Ratchet, lever and claw load binders for chain tie-downs, 1/4″ to 5/8″ chain, with WLL, proof and ultimate load for every size.

items.q: Ratchet or lever binder?
items.a: A ratchet binder tensions gradually and releases under control, so it suits operators who tension and release often. A lever binder is quicker but stores energy in the handle and must be released with care.

items.q: Are load binders lifting equipment?
items.a: No. A load binder tensions a chain tie-down to secure a load for transport. Its WLL is a tensioning rating and it is not for lifting.

items.q: Which fibre should I choose?
items.a: Polypropylene floats and is economical; polyethylene is similar and resists abrasion; nylon stretches and absorbs shock, which suits mooring; polyester stretches least and holds up best in sunlight. State the diameter, construction and length on the RFQ.

faqs.question: What is the working load limit?
faqs.answer: 2,600 to 13,000 lbs, depending on size, as the manufacturer rates it. The WLL is the most the part may carry in service; proof and breaking loads are test figures and never working limits.

faqs.question: Ratchet or lever binder?
faqs.answer: A ratchet binder tensions gradually and releases under control, so it suits operators who tension and release often. A lever binder is quicker but stores energy in the handle and must be released with care.

faqs.question: Are load binders lifting equipment?
faqs.answer: No. A load binder tensions a chain tie-down to secure a load for transport. Its WLL is a tensioning rating and it is not for lifting.

faqs.question: Ratchet or lever binder?
faqs.answer: A ratchet binder tensions gradually and releases under control, so it suits operators who tension and release often. A lever binder is quicker but stores energy in the handle and must be released with care.

faqs.question: Are load binders lifting equipment?
faqs.answer: No. A load binder tensions a chain tie-down to secure a load for transport. Its WLL is a tensioning rating and it is not for lifting.

products.descriptionShort: Light Double Snatch Block with Hook, 409 pattern, in 8 sizes, 4-1/2″ to 18″, WLL 4 to 15 t. Indus part numbers, manufacturer's test certificate.
products.descriptionLong:
Snatch blocks and pulley blocks change the direction of a rope or multiply a line pull. This range follows the 409 pattern.

Sizes and ratings

8 sizes, 4-1/2″ to 18″. Working load limit 4 to 15 t. Every size has its own Indus part number in the table below, with the loads in the unit the manufacturer rates them in.

Choosing a size

Rate the block for the load it actually sees: with the rope turned through 180° it carries about twice the line pull. Match the sheave to the rope diameter.

Ordering

Quote the Indus part number from the size table, or send the size and working load you need. Each consignment ships with the manufacturer's test certificate; say on the RFQ if your site needs anything more.
products.seoTitle: Light Double Snatch Block with Hook 409 Pattern
products.seoDescription: Light Double Snatch Block with Hook (409): 8 sizes, 4-1/2″ to 18″, WLL 4 to 15 t. Indus part numbers and test certificate. Request a quote.

faqs.question: What sizes does the light double snatch block with hook come in?
faqs.answer: 8 sizes, 4-1/2″ to 18″. The size table lists each one with its Indus part number, ratings and dimensions.

faqs.question: What is the working load limit?
faqs.answer: 4 to 15 t, depending on size, as the manufacturer rates it. The WLL is the most the part may carry in service; proof and breaking loads are test figures and never working limits.

faqs.question: Can a snatch block be used for lifting?
faqs.answer: Yes, within its rated load — but the load on the block is not the load on the rope. With the rope turned through 180° the block carries about twice the line pull, so rate the block, its hook or shackle and its anchor point for that.

faqs.question: Do the parts come with a test certificate?
faqs.answer: Yes. Each consignment ships with the manufacturer's test certificate. For third-party certification or witnessed proof testing, say so on the RFQ.

faqs.question: What do G-209, G-2130 and G-213 mean?
faqs.answer: They are widely used US pattern numbers: G-209 is a screw-pin anchor shackle, G-2130 a bolt-type anchor shackle, and G-213 a round-pin anchor shackle. Shackles sold to a pattern share its dimensions, so they interchange in an existing rigging plan.

faqs.question: What is the difference between WLL, SWL and breaking load?
faqs.answer: WLL — working load limit — is the most the manufacturer rates a part to carry in service. SWL, safe working load, is the older term and is sometimes set lower for a particular installation. The minimum breaking load is what the part withstood in test, several times its WLL, and it is never a working figure.

A shackle joins a sling, hook or chain to a lifting point and opens with a removable pin. This range follows the G-209 pattern, sized to interchange in an existing rigging plan.

Sizes and ratings

faqs.answer: 0.333 to 35 t, depending on size, as the manufacturer rates it. The WLL is the most the part may carry in service; proof and breaking loads are test figures and never working limits.

faqs.question: What do G-209, G-2130 and G-213 mean?
faqs.answer: They are widely used US pattern numbers: G-209 is a screw-pin anchor shackle, G-2130 a bolt-type anchor shackle, and G-213 a round-pin anchor shackle. Shackles sold to a pattern share its dimensions, so they interchange in an existing rigging plan.

faqs.question: What is the difference between WLL, SWL and breaking load?
faqs.answer: WLL — working load limit — is the most the manufacturer rates a part to carry in service. SWL, safe working load, is the older term and is sometimes set lower for a particular installation. The minimum breaking load is what the part withstood in test, several times its WLL, and it is never a working figure.

faqs.answer: Yes. Each consignment ships with the manufacturer's test certificate. For third-party certification or witnessed proof testing, say so on the RFQ.
